commenti.body:
It's been a while since I've seen it but I would agree with your analysis being a present theme throughout the film (from what I remember). I think the idea of escapism also goes a lot more personal and internalised. It's not just about an idea to escape the external reality we engage in but also a desire to escape who we are as an individual, right down to our core personality. This is demonstrated through the character Paprika herself who serves as an avatar for what her real world self (can't remember her name) wishes she could embody. What better way to change who you are internally in your mind than through entering your own subconscious? 

Thinking about this further I seem to recall this is the first thing we are watching when the movie starts. The male protagonist is inside his dream, trying to unlock a deep seated part of his memory in order to heal and change those parts of who they are.

The real world has damaged a part of themselves internally. In the dream world they can confront it.

As a side note I unfortunately saw this movie in '08/'09 around a time I first started experimenting with drugs and only a year or two before the release of Inception. I really like Inception, don't get me wrong, but Paprika completely ruined my expectations and desires for what I want out of a movie set in a dream scape. Inception kind of bugged me that none of the dream worlds they entered felt like an actual dream, and when it did it was only influenced by deliberate design of the characters and even then to a level no where near as fantastical as what Paprika envisioned. I know there's an argument to be made for the lack of constraints animation provides but I'm sure someone like Jadarowski could have conjured something much more surreal and dream like using practical effects.

film is rather clear on that , the villains and victims want it blur between but Paprika and our cop are clear on using dream to heal , to pave the daylife , those 2 explicitly want dream to end and move forward.

and that is why I dont get how you pull a "Many dont ever want a good movie to end" A story have an end , a good "thing" that dont end can be good to you , it just wont be a story.

>I really like Inception, don't get me wrong, but Paprika completely ruined my expectations and desires for what I want out of a movie set in a dream scape. Inception kind of bugged me that none of the dream worlds they entered felt like an actual dream

Inception's ending wouldn't work if the dreams were overly surreal.

There's tons of movies and TV shows that lean into the surreal possibilities of dreams. Inception sets itself apart in this regard imo.

That's a fair statement. For me personally after watching Paprika for the first time so close to Inception's release and knowing it would be set in a dream universe it gave an expectation and hope for what I was expecting that was ultimately unfulfilled. I dream every time I go to sleep and no part of Inception resembled dreams to me. I still enjoyed the movie a lot, and I understand what you mean that if the dreams were too obvious then the ending of "is this reality?" wouldn't work the same way, but it still left me wanting something more.

I think the ending was also a bit of a let down for me as well as it was around that time I saw Existenz for the first time. As a result it was very quickly into the movie, possibly before even going in to see it, that I thought to myself "is this going to end with a 'is this still a dream or not?' twist". Especially given Existenz shared a similar "fake reality inside a fake reality inside a fake reality" concept. This was probably also helped by Memento and Prestige having twists so it was probably also an expectation I had of the director at the time.

>I dream every time I go to sleep and no part of Inception resembled dreams to me. 

Ha. The dreams that I remember are usually pretty mundane. 

>As a result it was very quickly into the movie, possibly before even going in to see it, that I thought to myself "is this going to end with a 'is this still a dream or not?' twist". 

It's a fairly common trope now. A lot of horror movies end with that "was it all in their head?" shtick. Total Recall is a classic example. 

I think with Inception, the film still works because the ending isn't built around that twist.
Yeah that's true. A lot of my impression probably just comes down to the time I watched it too.
I thought my dreams are getting pretty boring too cus I m. but funny that I like flying in it so much I m having more of them so I dont need to learn lucid for now ha

I just finished the book, having seen the anime a couple of years ago.

So my perspective now is from the novel which I did not really like. The Japanese names make it difficult to follow at times.  The main theme is the intrigue and politics at the psychiatric institute. This becomes quite tedious. Only after 2/3 of the novel the surreal intrusion of the dream world in real life starts.
 It is also quite sexist, paprika is almost raped but lets it go because the attacker is handsome. She is attracted by all powerful men she meets, it feels like a male fantasy. Same problem I have with hausu. 

The movie is much better because it focusses on the reality dream dichotomy. It is truely excellent in depicting the mind bending dream scenes. Could not be done in a real action movie I think.
I will rewatch soon.

I agree with your analysis, and also think this is a throughline in Kon’s work — the relationship between reality and fantasy is also crucial to Perfect Blue and Millennium Actress. I was going to say that Paprika newly brings in the internet as part of this theme but actually the internet plays a critical role in Perfect Blue too!

I admire how the fantastical in these stories is never villainized despite Kon being pretty unambiguously critical of the escapist impulse (even in something like Millennium Actress, which is profoundly bittersweet, I feel like you’re left wondering if all that fantasy was “worth it”)… it feels reflective of art-making too. An artist clearly in love with creativity and imagination and fantasy, with powerful skills in that arena of his own, who is also articulating ambivalence about those very human desires and capacities.
